Multi-Touch Marketing Checklist For Canvassing
Use this checklist to “crack open” a neighborhood. This works for making your first sale, or just moving into a new neighborhood. Remember, persistence pays off! Hit the same homes 3-5 times before moving on.

NOTE: If you have any leads that come in through the office, send the New Lead Confirmation Email right away!

• Use the Paperless Canvassing Tracker to document the date, time, address, and outcome of every door you knock.  Or print this one Printable Canvassing Tracker.
• Knock doors in the targeted neighborhood using the SLAP Canvassing Formula.
• If no one is home, leave the Door Hanger Letter
• At the end of the day, send a Direct Mail Letter (see list of letters to choose from) in the mail to every house where no one was home (pick the one that’s most relevant to the situation)
• Show back up at the houses you knocked where no one was home (left letter and sent letter in the mail). Use SLAP Canvassing Formula
• If no one is home, leave the Sorry I Missed You direct mail letter.
• At the end of the day, send the Follow Up Direct Mail Letter in the mail to every house where no one was home (pick the one that’s most relevant to the situation)
• Show back up at the houses you knocked where no one was home (left letter and sent letter in the mail). Use SLAP Canvassing Formula
• Follow up with ALL leads who you didn’t close using the Follow Up Templates

docs.body:
My 12-Step Sales Process

From Inspection to Sale: How to Get Invited Inside to Close the Sale!

The goal of your inspection is to give the homeowner something to visualize, see, touch, and feel. Educate them on what you see, why it’s important, and what they should do next.

Step 1: Walk the perimeter of the home (I always do it clockwise so it’s the same every time).

Inspect for shingle granules coming out of downspouts. Look for roofing debris or signs of missing shingles in the yard. Take photos and videos.

Step 2: Inspect the roof.

Inspect from the ladder first. How many layers? Is there ice and water shield? Are the gutters installed correctly? Any issues with gutter protection? Inspect all flashings and roof penetrations. Inspect for adequate ventilation. Inspect the field shingles. Take pictures and videos of anything you find.  Link below has a full inspection process.

Inspection: The BRN Way

Step 3: Climb down and ask the homeowner where you can sit down and show them what you found.

Explain to the homeowner that you have photos and videos to share on your phone and that it will be easiest if you can get out of the sun. “Where can we go to review these photos and videos out of the sun so you can see my screen?” Usually they will invite you inside. Have them look at your phone and explain what each of the photos and videos is showing them.

Step 4: Educate the homeowner on their options.

I always start with this quote. “I’m going to explain what your options are and what I recommend you do whether you work with me or someone else. Because the truth is, you can choose anyone you want to help with this process. Of course I’d love to earn your business, but most importantly, I want to make sure you feel comfortable and confident with the decision you choose.”

Then move on to explaining how the process works, how you can help, and what they should expect throughout the process.

Step 5: Ask if they have any questions.

It’s important to get the objections out of the way. This is all about THEM. Notice that we haven’t started talking about YOU yet. Keep it focused on education and value.

Once all their questions are satisfied, it’s time to switch to the pitch.

Step 6: Pitch!

Now is your time to showcase your value and help them choose you. This is your opportunity to bust out any testimonials, reviews, and name drop other homeowners in the neighborhood first. Before you talk about the company, start here. It’s familiar ground and makes them feel comfortable.

Then talk about what makes YOU and your company different. Is it your attention to detail? 1-day installation? Warranty? Ability to tackle all the trades? Give your prospect one core concept to hang on to so they think to themselves, “Hey, that guy is better because _________.”

To get my entire sales presentation using my CARPARK Closing Formula, use this.

Step 7: Set up for the close.

Before asking for the business, we want the prospect to “sell themselves.” It’s important to get them talking. I like to ask a question like this, “So, after seeing the condition of your roof and now that you understand HOW the process works, can I ask you a question? What is the most important thing for you when it comes to choosing a contractor [or roofer]?

LET THEM TALK. Do not say a word. Let them explain what they’re looking for.

Then respond, “Well, you’re in luck! You just described [COMPANY NAME] and how I work.” So let me ask you just one more question…

Step 8: Ask for the business.

Now you want to repeat back to your prospect exactly what they told you they’re looking for in a contractor by using the “if, then” close (reference this video).

“Great, [THEIR NAME]. So if I could [REPEAT BACK WHAT THEY TOLD YOU THEY ARE LOOKING FOR], then would you feel comfortable choosing me to handle this entire process for you?”

Step 9: Don’t say a word until they speak!

At this point, you don’t say a word. This is a “close ended” question that will result in a simple “Yes” or “No.” Don’t be surprised if a homeowner comes at you with another objection. That’s OK. They may say something like. “I think so, but I have to chat with my husband” or “I’m not sure yet, I want to speak with a couple other roofers.”

If they don’t say “YES,” then your next move is to overcome those objections, or set the follow up.

Remember to use the follow-up techniques and scripts inside your Marketing Battle Pack.

If they say YES, it’s time to move onto the paperwork.

Step 10: Transition to your paperwork.

First rule of thumb. NEVER EVER call it a contract. It freaks people out. Call it “paperwork” or an “agreement” or “paperwork.”

Explain what the paperwork says before showing them so they don’t panic when they see something they need to sign.

Also, never ask them to “sign.” Ask them to “execute” or “autograph.”

Step 11: Collect their email address and insurance agent info.

Never leave the house without all the contact info. You’ll want to use their email address and insurance agent email address to use the “Insurance Agent Referral” emails and “Customer Project Update” emails (which also ask for referrals).

Step 12: Set clear expectations about what happens next.

Homeowners always want to know what’s next. Explain the next 3 steps very clearly. Who will be in contact with them next, and when?

Also, make sure to set up your next appointment or call so they know exactly when they’ll hear from you. Skittish customers jump ship and cancel. Now is your chance to provide kick butt service they’ll never forget! Do this, and get more referrals.

BONUS STEPS

Bonus 1: Before you leave the house ASK FOR INTRODUCTIONS/REFERRALS.

If it feels right (and sometimes it is too soon), be sure to ask for introductions. You can do it like this. “Hey [CUSTOMER NAME], I’m so glad we met. This has been really enjoyable and I’m super excited about helping you throughout the process, aren’t you? [WAIT FOR AN AGREEMENT]. I’m glad to hear that! While I’m here, I’d love to provide the same level of service to your neighbors. Do you know any of them? [WAIT FOR THEIR RESPONSE]. Do you have a quick minute to introduce me to any of them? [WAIT FOR THEIR RESPONSE].”

At this point they will offer to walk you over there, or you can at least ask for their names to make it easier to knock the door. That way when you knock the door you can address the homeowner by name and tell them that your new customer (mention them by name) referred you to them.

Bonus 2: Go sign up the neighbors using “warm” door knocking.

Before you leave the neighborhood, it’s time to canvass the neighbors using the SLAP Formula! Go knock all the doors you can immediately surrounding the house. You have a GREAT reason to show up “warm” and use the name of the person you just signed up to sign more neighbors. Remember to point to the home of your new customer as you knock doors to really create a warm, friendly, and trustworthy first impression.

  prospect’s needs and desires.

  Great, so now we theoretically captured their
  attention, and they gave us the time of day to
  explain what we do and how we can help.

 Now what?  How do you get to the kitchen table?

  Use these 3 tricks, and you’ll be sure to

 Ask questions.

   Ask questions.
When you show up at the door, end your quick pitch with a question
such as, “what damage have you noticed?” or “has your insurance
company been out yet?” or “what prompted you to give us a call to
come out?” Nine times out of 10, if you ask a question, you will get
much more information in return. This will help you with trick #2!

   Determine what stage of the claims process.
There are 4 Stages of the Claims Process that The Roof Strategist teaches. 1.
No claim 2. Partial pay 3. Denial 4. Check in hand. If you listen closely to the
way your prospect answers your questions, you will have a clear insight into
which stage they are in. Each of these stages has unique needs and desires.
A homeowner with their check in hand does not need a free inspection! Be
sure your pitch speaks directly to their needs and desires. If they are
intrigued and recognize the need for your services, they will invite you in!

   Show photos & videos from your phone as an
  excuse to get out of the sun.
During your inspection or walkthrough you should be taking photos. This
provides tangible value to the prospect. They can see, touch, and feel when
you put the photos in their hands. I’d even recommend doing a short 30-60
second video while you’re up on the roof. Be sure to document something
above and beyond what they think you’re up there looking for. Maybe it’s
the kids frisbee on a roof or gutters that are clogged up. When you get off
the roof you pull out your iPad or phone to go through the pictures. “It’s
awfully hard to see these pictures with the sun glaring off the screen. Where
would be a good place for us to sit down and review these photos where
we’re not in the sun?” You now have a reason to passively invite yourself in.
These techniques work because they bring value and peak the prospect’s
interest so they can literally see what you are talking about. As soon as you
hit the kitchen table, the energy of the sale shifts greatly in your favor!

 increase your kitchen table conversion rate!

Remember, ask questions, find out what stage of the claims process they
are in, and take photos as an excuse to get out of the sun and sit at the
kitchen table. Close deals in the comfort of your prospect’s home by
delivering value that directly speaks to their immediate needs and desires.

Use this formula to create your own “pitch” at the door. This works for storm and retail. I recommend printing this out and keeping it with you.

The “S.L.A.P” Formula To Pitch On The Fly!

What It Means
Sample
S
Say hi and break the ice
“Hey, I’m Adam. Beautiful boat in the driveway by the way…”
L
Let them know why you’re here. Make it familiar to their neighborhood, neighbors street, or subdivision.
“I just left your neighbor Peggy’s house after helping her ______. The reason I’m here is to…”
A
Ask an open ended question (that requires them to think about an answer. NOT a “yes” or “no”
“How has the insurance process been for you?” -OR- “When was the last time your roof was inspected and had routine maintenance?”
P
Present your pitch in response to their answer.
“I understand. Good news I stopped by because ....”

This strategy works best by getting the insurance agent name/email from every single customer. If you build just 1 relationship, the agent could refer customers to you for years!

This script is for cold outreach to new insurance agents. The best way to find insurance agents is to use Google Search or LinkedIn. Search for residential and/or commercial property insurance.

Call Script

These services include:

• Status updates on the claim (including photographs if requested)
• Construction updates
• Photographs for the client’s file

The insurance agents we work with really value our approach.

Is this type of service relationship something you’d be interested in?

Introduction

This easy “template” will help you knock doors and ace your pitch. Remember, all you need to do is start a conversation!

It addresses your target market, problems you solve, and immediate desires you fulfill with your product/services.

Understanding The Basics

• Your target market is the group of people you serve most of the time. Who are they?

• The problem(s) you solve is the fundamental purpose of your product or services.
• Problems of the Storm Restoration target market often include:
• Provide free inspections to identify damage
• Repair/Replace damaged roofing, siding, windows & gutters
• Get insufficiently paid claims increased
• Get denied claims approved
• The immediate desires of a customer are those longing feelings that your target market experiences that prompt them to search for your services.
• We must sell them what they want to buy. Not what we are selling.
• Immediate desires of the Storm Restoration target market often include:
• I want my property fixed right away because I’m afraid my roof will leak.
• I want to find out if my house got damaged.
• I want someone to handle this for me because I don’t have time.
• I don’t want this storm to cost me a lot of money.
• I want to find a quality contractor that I can trust.
• Note: The more you can propose emotional and financial solutions, the more powerful your statement will be. Remember, people buy results and feelings, not products!

Make a list for each of the three categories (target market, problems, & desires).

Step 2
Plug and play the appropriate combinations for that prospect.

docs.title: Selling Secrets: Needs vs. Desires
docs.summary: Selling Secrets: Understanding Needs and Desires **People only buy the things they need or want!**
docs.body:
Selling Secrets:
Understanding Needs and Desires
**People only buy the things they need or want!**

A property owner experiences storm damage.... What do they need and want?

What is a Need?

• A solution to a problem
• Usually a remedy/fix
• Can’t live without it
• An objective experience
• Example: You get a flat tire on the side of the highway. You need your tire changed.

What is a Desire?

• The impulse that makes you take action
• Something you want
• An emotional experience
• Example: You need a new car because your transmission blew. You want to start shopping for a luxury truck.

So… What’s the difference between Needs and Desires?

Needs are the root of the problem that require a solution. Desires are the choices we make in finding the solution that make us happy.

Example: My roof had shingles blow off and is leaking into my bedroom. Need = Fix leaking roof. Desire = I want my roof fixed quickly, affordably, and by a reputable company.

See… many options are usually available to fill the need, but fewer are available for the desire.

To sell effectively, we must understand the specific needs and desires of our prospect based on where they are in the 4 Stages of the Claims Process.

#1 No Claim  -  #2 Partial Pay  -  #3 Denial  -  #4 Check in Hand

Roofer vs. Storm Restoration Contractor

Now that we know our prospect’s Needs and Desires, we can start to explain who we are and how we can help.

When does a homeowner need a roofer?
• When they are ready to install a roof

So… what happens if they haven't filed a claim? Didn’t get full coverage by the insurance company? Got denied coverage?

The only way to get a commitment (contingency agreement) to do business together is to have the Solution to their Needs and Desires.

If we position ourselves properly as a Storm Restoration Contractor, it envelops the skills a roofer has, plus creates the need to use your services NOW versus waiting for when they may, or may not, be ready to install a roof.

What Needs and Desires does a Roofer fulfill?
• Putting on a roof
• Roof repairs

What Needs and Desires does a Storm Restoration Contractor fulfill?
• Save time
• Save money
• Meet with insurance company
• Ensure proper and full assessment of damages
• Handle claim from start to finish
• Replace roof
• Warranty roof
• Make sure price doesn’t exceed deductible
• Insurance policy expertise
• Xactimate expertise

So… Who do you want working on your storm damage claim? A Roofer or Storm Restoration Contractor?

A Roofer tries his best to serve his prospect in hopes of being chosen to repair or replace the roof.

A Storm Restoration Contractor uses his insurance expertise, Xactimate expertise, claims handling knowledge, and roofing knowledge to accurately and fully assess damage and then replace said damages.

The only way to get a prospect to sign with you is if they Need you now!

docs.body:
Pitch Book Template

Use this template to build your own pitch book! You can print everything out and put it in a 3-ring binder. Or you can create a digital copy using Powerpoint, Google Slides, or your favorite slide building program.

Watch this video to learn how to use your new pitch book: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ts6wLLBnfd8

Put Your “Pitch Book” Together in Order Like This...

Introduction Letter
This section should be a short, personal letter. Make it about the customer and your commitment to helping them. This is how you win over their heart and their mind.

SAMPLE LETTER YOU CAN USE/EDIT

Dear Homeowner,

Thank you for your time today. I value the opportunity to earn your business.

Choosing a contractor can be difficult.

You likely have a ton of questions including, “Who will do the best work?” or “Who will stand behind their work?” or “Who will give me the best value?”

During our time together, I’ll answer these questions to help you make the decision that’s best for you.

Because the truth is, you can choose any contractor you’d like.

My goal is to become your first choice by:  -Listening to your questions and concerns
-Helping you understand the entire process from start to finish
-Giving you a 5-star worthy experience that you’d want to tell your friends about

As I share this information with you, please interrupt me with questions at any time.

I want you to feel comfortable and confident with whatever choice you make - even if it’s not with me.

Respectfully,

[YOUR NAME]

Testimonials
Include screenshots from your public reviews on Google, Facebook, Home Advisor, etc. You can also use screenshots or printed out text messages and emails from customers. The more authentic looking the better. You can copy/paste the text as a last resort.

List of Addresses in the Neighborhood You’ve Worked
Include a list of property addresses of installs you’ve done in the area. Only use names if customers give you permission. This shows even more credibility that you’re the “neighborhood” roofer. If you don’t have addresses in that specific area, you can use some from the surrounding area.

Certification and Statistics
Include any certifications from shingle manufacturers. Include any other noteworthy certifications or affiliations. You can also include the statistics about the business such as: How long you’ve been in business and how many roofs you’ve installed.

Licenses and Insurance Information
If licensing is required in your state, include a copy of your state or local licenses. You may wish to include a copy of your insurance information as well. This information makes homeowners feel like they are in good hands working with a professional company.

Sample Warranty
Put in sample warranties for your workmanship and/or the shingle manufacturer warranties. If you provide or offer extended warranty options, this is where you want to showcase them as an option. This can act as a type of “primer” to upsell the warranty later.

Process Overview

• Color Selection
• Show samples of the shingle lines you offer. If you offer multiple shingle manufacturers, include all logos. Include all types of shingles and any upsell or upgrade options. This is great for “priming” the upsell or upgrade later.
• Scheduling
• Explain the scheduling process. Who will call them. Who will email them. How it works. This is a great time to share safety guidelines about the installation.
• Delivery
• Show a picture of material getting delivered. You can showcase rooftop delivery or driveway delivery.

• Prep
• Show a picture of a house being prepped for installation. Plywood over garage doors/windows. Gardens covered with tarps. Etc.
• Install
• Show a picture of your crew working.
• Walkthrough and Invoicing
• Include a sample of your final walkthrough checklist. Put the homeowner at ease knowing the job will be inspected upon completion.
• Before and After Photos
• Include 5-10 homes of before and after photos.

Questions?
Include a page or slide with just the word “Questions?” on it. This will invite your homeowner to ask questions. Once they run out of questions, it’s time to transition to your close and ask for the business.

Even though we’ve finished your project we aren’t done serving you. We’ve helped lots of homeowners, even after their projects are complete, make sure they are educated and prepared in the event they have another claim.

Below you’ll find 3 suggestions to protect your home and get the most out of your insurance coverage. Give your agent a call today to make sure your policy doesn’t leave you exposed if you have another claim. Sometimes the fine print can be an unfortunate surprise.

1. Matching endorsement. Let’s say in 8 years you experience another [HAIL STORM/WIND EVENT/HURRICANE/STORM] that damages your roof. The shingle manufacturer may have discontinued the color you selected and an exact match cannot be found.

If the insurance company determines that only part of your roof is damaged, you may be forced to repair the roof and now have 2 different color shingles. The only way to avoid this would be to come out of pocket to cover the rest so it all looks the same.

With a matching endorsement your insurance policy would cover the difference to maintain a uniform look for your roofing, siding, paint, etc.

2. Coverage exclusions. Insurance companies have been writing crafty language to avoid paying for certain types of claims. Here are a few exclusions to watch out for.

• Exclusions for hail or wind coverage
• Limited coverage after the roof is a certain age
• Partial coverage payment versus “replacement cost value”

3.  Actual Cash Value (ACV) vs. Replacement Cost Value (RCV). Actual cash value (ACV) means paying for what the damaged building products are worth today. With an ACV policy you could be left with a huge out-of-pocket expense for home repairs. Example: If your roof costs $10,000 to replace and is already 9 years old, the insurance company will only pay a portion of the cost at a prorated amount. You may only get $4,000 and have to cover the difference yourself.

Replacement cost value (RCV) means the insurance company will pay for a brand new roof minus your deductible. Many people don’t realize what type of coverage they have until after a claim. Make sure you don’t have any surprises and be sure you have a Replacement Cash Value policy.

Subject: Myth vs. Fact About Choosing a Contractor

[HOMEOWNER],

I’m sharing this to help you choose a contractor.

Many homeowners think that property damage claims are handled similar to an auto claim, but they aren’t.

The truth is you have the right to choose any contractor that you like and that you trust.

Price should not be a factor when it comes to an insurance claim.

Here are a few myths vs. facts to “set the record straight” when it comes to the insurance process.

Myth: Your insurance company needs estimates.

Fact: Regardless of the contractor you choose to work with, the insurance company will write their own estimate based on their property assessment.

The estimate will be prepared on a third party estimating program. These “prices” are updated monthly by zip code and set by a third party.

There is zero “price” negotiation.

The only negotiation is regarding actual assessment of damaged building materials based on quantity, type of installation, and building code requirements.

Myth: Your insurance company will tell you which contractor to choose.

Fact: By law you are allowed to select the contractor that you like.

The insurance company will pay the exact amount on their assessment no matter who you choose to do the work.

Myth: You should get estimates and select the cheapest contractor to save money.

Fact: Believe it or not, there is more than one way to write an estimate on a roof.

Pricing depends on material choices, type of installation, and if certain materials on the roof will be reused or replaced with new.

The “cheapest” contractor is likely not completing all the work on the insurance estimate or reusing certain building materials.

You run the risk of getting an inferior installation that will cost you more over the lifespan of the roof.

Price should not be a deciding factor for your project, as the insurance company has fixed the pricing structure based on their third party estimating program.

Be sure to select a contractor who will do all the work listed by the insurance assessment.

Myth: If you get the work done for cheaper than the insurance estimate, you can keep the rest.

Fact: The insurance company will pay a portion of the claim up front.

This is called the “Actual Cash Value” (ACV) payment.

The remaining balance of the claim (called “depreciation”) will be paid only once the work is complete and the insurance company has been invoiced proving that all the work was done as per the insurance estimate.

The only legal way to obtain the “depreciation” is to provide evidence to the insurance company that the work was completed.

Typically, the insurance company will require an invoice with a dollar amount.

If you select a contractor who has done the work for less than the insurance amount one of two things can happen.

• The insurance company only releases “depreciation” up to the actual invoice amount. This means that you are not able to keep the “leftover” money as it will not be sent.
• If the contractor falsifies the invoice amount to the insurance company, both you and the contractor are participating in fraud.

Tips to Choose a Contractor

Be sure to select a contractor that meets the following criteria.

• Understands insurance policy language
• Properly assesses your property damage
• Understands insurance industry estimating programs
• Will review and complete all work as agreed upon on the insurance assessment
• Will invoice the insurance company directly once all work is complete

If you’re still in the process of choosing a contractor, I’d be happy to help.
